content:
Apple has asked the court hearing its lawsuit to allow its appointed experts direct access to defendants' forensic image files, and to obtain documents related to OpenAI's hardware development. Details below.

A little background

In early July this year, Apple filed suit against a former employee, OpenAI, and io Products, alleging misappropriation of trade secrets.

The lawsuit involves former Apple employees alleged to have taken confidential information when leaving the company. Apple alleges that former employee Chang Liu provided interview coaching to another Apple employee before that person interviewed at OpenAI, and that Tang Tan directed candidates applying for Apple positions to bring materials such as hardware components to their interviews.

Earlier, Apple said preliminary forensic results showed that the MacBook Liu used after leaving the company had been used during his OpenAI tenure to run a simulation test involving Apple confidential schematics. Apple also said the MacBook's records showed Liu had used a Mac mini, which the company later sought access to in the case.

OpenAI subsequently pushed back against Apple's claims, saying the situation was "Apple's own doing" because Apple's purported offboarding and security procedures were too lax, allowing employees to inadvertently retain access to confidential information after departure.

One point of contention in the case is Apple's motion to expedite discovery, which OpenAI opposes. Another is Apple's request for an injunction that would, during the litigation, restrict OpenAI from using trade secrets it allegedly misappropriated — a move that could affect OpenAI's ongoing hardware development work.

Apple argues that, because OpenAI is still developing hardware products, certain discovery needs to be expedited, as the Apple trade secrets allegedly used risk becoming further commingled with that product development, making restoration to their original state increasingly difficult.

OpenAI countered that Apple had failed to explain why a separate expedited discovery track was needed, and called Apple's demands overly broad.

After the parties reached an impasse, the court ordered them to submit a joint letter outlining their respective positions on expedited discovery. That letter was filed last Friday and has since been unsealed.

Apple seeks forensic images and development records

In the joint letter, Apple asked the court to allow its forensic expert to directly access the raw forensic image files relied on by the defendants' expert, in order to analyze Liu's devices and determine whether he accessed or used Apple confidential information after leaving.

Apple said its forensic expert had identified what it called "material flaws" in the defendants' expert's analysis, and argued its expert must be given direct access to the files to determine whether the defendants' forensic analysis has additional problems.

Below is Apple's statement:

Apple's forensic expert has identified numerous material flaws in the defendants' expert's analysis, including: (1) failure to locate files that were clearly used and stored on Liu's Mac mini; and (2) incorrectly concluding that zero-byte files or files with an empty kMDItemLastUsedDate field on the Mac mini had never been accessed. ⋯⋯ Giving Apple's expert direct access to these forensic images is essential to understanding what other errors the defendants' expert may have made.

OpenAI argued that Apple's expert should not be given unlimited access to the forensic images, and proposed instead that a neutral forensic expert handle the images under a process agreed by both sides.

Apple countered that such an arrangement would put it at a disadvantage, because the defendants' own forensic expert already has direct access to the material.

Beyond the forensic material, Apple is also seeking expedited access to documents related to OpenAI's hardware development, including development records on metal surface finishes, power management, and battery functionality.

OpenAI had earlier argued that its metal surface finish technology was developed independently and did not use Apple confidential information, and that the simulation test Liu ran using Apple confidential files was unrelated to its upcoming product.

Apple is now seeking the underlying development records to verify those claims; OpenAI said this is nothing more than an attempt to "spy on a competitor."

The joint letter also addressed a number of other points of contention, including:

  • Apple further sought forensic images of devices currently or previously used by Liu, Tan, former Apple employee Yu-Ting "Alyssa" Peng, and another OpenAI employee, provided those devices currently or previously contained what Apple defined as "Apple-derived data";
  • Records of Liu's use of AI tools — defendants had earlier said the forensic investigation found no evidence he used Apple confidential files on platforms such as ChatGPT, Codex, Claude, or OpenClaw;
  • Documents from OpenAI's consumer hardware product division related to interviews, including materials actually used during interviews and communications with departing Apple employees;
  • OpenAI said some of the inquiries could affect more than 400 former Apple employees currently working at OpenAI.

Apple is also seeking the complete LINE conversation records between Liu and Peng, including messages in which Peng asked Liu technical questions about her Apple work after he left the company.

Defendants, in opposing Apple's injunction motion, submitted excerpts of those conversations, but Apple argued it should be allowed access to the full conversations, not just the portions defendants produced.
